questions.q: How is every JavaScript number stored?
questions.explain: All numbers share one format, integers included. The 53 significant bits decide where integers stop being exact.
options: As a 32-bit integer when it has no fraction, otherwise as a decimal
As a 64-bit IEEE 754 double: a sign bit, 11 exponent bits and 52 fraction bits (53 significant bits)

questions.q: Why is 0.1 not stored exactly?
questions.explain: Just as 1/3 has no finite decimal form, 1/10 has no finite binary form. The stored value is slightly above 0.1.
options: In binary, 1/10 is an infinitely repeating fraction, so it is rounded to the nearest value that fits in 53 significant bits
Because of a bug in V8
It is stored exactly; only printing is wrong

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Printing shows the shortest decimal that maps back to the same double, 0.1. Asking for 20 significant digits reveals the stored value, a little above 0.1.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Above 253 the gap between doubles is 2, so 253 + 1 rounds back to 253. That is why 253 itself is not "safe": another integer rounds to it.

questions.q: Number.isInteger(2 ** 60) is true. Why is it still wrong to trust 2 ** 60 as an exact order id?
questions.explain: isInteger only asks "is there a fraction?". isSafeInteger also asks "is this the only integer with this representation?".
options: It has no fractional part, but it is far beyond 2<sup>53</sup>, so many different integers round to the same double
Because it is stored as a bigint

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.parse converts every number to a double. 9007199254740993 is not representable, so it becomes its even neighbour, silently.

questions.q: What is Number.EPSILON?
questions.explain: It is the spacing of doubles near 1. The spacing grows with magnitude, so it is not a universal tolerance. The smallest positive number is Number.MIN_VALUE.
options: The smallest positive number JavaScript can store
The gap between 1 and the next larger double, about 2.2 × 10<sup>-16</sup>
A tolerance that works for comparing any two numbers
The largest safe integer divided by 2

questions.q: Why does Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON fail to treat 1e20 + 30000 and 1e20 as nearly equal?
questions.explain: Scale the tolerance with the values, for example relative * Math.max(|a|, |b|).
options: Near 10<sup>20</sup> neighbouring doubles are thousands apart, so a fixed tiny tolerance can never match; a tolerance relative to the size of the numbers is needed
Because Math.abs does not work on large numbers

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every addition rounds, and different orders round differently. 0.1 + 0.2 is already 0.30000000000000004, and adding 0.3 gives 0.6000000000000001; the other order happens to land on 0.6.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Dividing by zero gives Infinity; NaN is never equal to itself; Object.is distinguishes -0 from 0; and the maximum of nothing is -Infinity.

questions.q: An API receives {"quantity": 1e308} and later {"quantity": "5"}. Which check rejects both as quantities?
questions.explain: 1e308 is a number but not a safe integer; "5" is a string, and Number.isSafeInteger does not coerce. typeof would accept 1e308, NaN and Infinity.

questions.q: A refund of −0.001 naira is shown to a customer. What does this print?
questions.explain: toFixed keeps the sign of a tiny negative, printing "-0.00". Math.round(-0.4) is negative zero; String prints it as "0", but Object.is sees it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Math.round rounds halves towards +∞, so −2.5 becomes −2. toFixed rounds halves away from zero, so it gives "−3".

questions.q: A refund of −7 kobo is split between 2 accounts with integer division. What does this print?
questions.explain: trunc drops the fraction (towards zero), floor goes down (towards −∞). % keeps the sign of the left side, which matches trunc: −7 = 2 × −3 + −1.

questions.q: Why do many accounting systems prefer round half to even?
questions.explain: Always rounding halves up adds a small bias every time. Half-even removes that bias on average: 2.5 → 2, 3.5 → 4.
options: It always rounds in the customer's favour
Exact halves go up half the time and down half the time, so totals over many transactions do not drift upwards
It is the only rounding mode JavaScript supports

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The stored 1.005 is slightly less than 1.005, so both the product and the value toFixed rounds are just below the half. Rounding afterwards cannot fix a number that is already on the wrong side.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toFixed rounds the stored double (just below 1.005). Intl.NumberFormat starts from the shortest decimal for that double, "1.005", and rounds half away from zero. Two formatters, two answers: round your kobo once yourself.
questions.code:
const twoDecimals = new Intl.NumberFormat("en", { minimumFractionDigits: 2, maximumFractionDigits: 2 });
console.log((1.005).toFixed(2), twoDecimals.format(1.005));

questions.q: A function decides rounding by comparing 2 * remainder with the denominator, all in whole kobo. What is the advantage over Math.round(numerator / denominator)?
questions.explain: With integers there is no representation error, so an exact half is recognised as exactly half and the rule you chose is the rule that runs.
options: "Less than half", "exactly half" and "more than half" are decided exactly with integers, so the chosen mode (half-even, half away from zero) is applied correctly even for exact halves
It works for any floating-point input

questions.q: An empty price field and a price with a comma arrive. What does this print?
questions.explain: Number turns an empty string and null into 0, which would make a product free. parseFloat stops at the comma and reads 1. Neither is safe for money.

questions.q: Why does a safe money parser split "1250.50" at the point and build 1250 * 100 + 50 instead of computing Math.round(parseFloat("1250.50") * 100)?
questions.explain: "1.005" × 100 shows the problem. With the text approach, no fraction is ever stored in a double.
options: Converting the decimal text to a double and multiplying can land just below a half and round the wrong way; building from digit strings uses only exact integers
Because multiplication is slower than addition

questions.q: A cashier types "1.005". What should a strict naira parser do?
questions.explain: Whatever happens to sub-kobo input must be a visible decision. Silent rounding hides typing mistakes and wrong data feeds.
options: Reject it (or apply a documented business rule), because kobo have two decimals and a third means the input is not an amount

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Arithmetic never mixes bigint and number silently. Comparisons across the types are allowed, but === also compares types, so it is false.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Bigint division truncates towards zero. Any other rounding must be written by hand with the remainder.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The number literal was rounded before BigInt saw it. Converting from a string keeps every digit.

questions.q: What does JSON.stringify({ total: 5n }) do?
questions.explain: JSON readers elsewhere might round a large integer, so JavaScript refuses by default. Use a replacer that turns bigints into strings (or JSON.rawJSON digits).
options: Throws a TypeError: it does not know how to serialise a BigInt

questions.q: What is the best way for an API to send a 64-bit order id in JSON?
questions.explain: Ids are labels, not quantities. Strings keep every digit in every language; large payment and messaging APIs do exactly this.
options: As a JSON number, because it is a number in the database
As a JSON string, "orderId": "1844674407370955169", so no JSON reader can round it
Split into two numbers, high and low
As a floating-point number with a decimal point

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The reviver's third argument gives the original source text of a number. Returning it keeps the id as an exact string.

questions.q: A function sums kobo amounts and the total passes Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. What does the lesson's sumKobo do, and why?
questions.explain: The rare huge-total case should be handled by code designed for it (a bigint path), not discovered later in a reconciliation report.
options: Switches silently to bigint, so callers never notice
Throws a RangeError, because a total that might be off by a kobo must be loud, and returning a number sometimes and a bigint other times would burden every caller
Rounds to the nearest thousand naira

questions.q: Why create new Intl.NumberFormat("en-NG", { style: "currency", currency: "NGN" }) once at module level?
questions.explain: The same applies to every Intl object: build once, call format many times.
options: Because each formatter can only format one number
Creating a formatter loads locale data and resolves options; reusing one avoids repeating that work for every amount
Because formatters are global and cannot be created twice
So that its rounding changes the stored amounts

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The en-NG locale uses the naira sign, commas for thousands, a point for decimals, and the currency's two decimals.
questions.code:
const naira = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-NG", { style: "currency", currency: "NGN" });
console.log(naira.format(1234567.5), naira.format(-2500));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Percent style multiplies by 100. Pass the fraction (0.075) for 7.5%.
questions.code:
const percent = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-NG", { style: "percent", maximumFractionDigits: 1 });
console.log(percent.format(0.075), percent.format(7.5));

questions.q: Why does formatKobo build a decimal string such as "90071992547409.93" and pass it to format, instead of passing kobo / 100?
questions.explain: For amounts near the safe limit, kobo / 100 is already off by a kobo before formatting. Integer division and remainder produce an exact string.
options: Dividing a large kobo value by 100 produces an approximate double, while Intl.NumberFormat formats a decimal string (or a bigint) exactly
Because strings format faster than numbers

questions.q: A shop starts selling in Japanese yen as well as naira. What changes about "minor units"?
questions.explain: resolvedOptions().maximumFractionDigits of a currency formatter reports the decimals: 2 for NGN, 0 for JPY, 3 for KWD.
options: Nothing: every currency has 100 minor units
The yen has no minor unit (0 decimals), so amounts must be stored with their currency and the number of decimals looked up per currency
Yen amounts must be stored as floats

questions.q: Which is the right source for a 6-digit one-time password sent by SMS?
questions.explain: Math.random is predictable given enough outputs. Anything an attacker must not guess needs a secure random source.
options: A cryptographically secure generator, such as crypto.getRandomValues or Node's crypto.randomInt(0, 1e6)
The last six digits of the order id

questions.q: The pg driver returns a PostgreSQL bigint column such as amount_kobo as the string "125050". Why, and what should your code do?
questions.explain: The driver cannot know whether your values stay in the safe range, so it hands you the exact digits and lets you choose.
options: It is a bug; call parseFloat on every value
A 64-bit integer may not fit a double exactly, so the driver refuses to round it; convert deliberately, for example with Number(value) after checking Number.isSafeInteger, or with BigInt(value)
Strings are faster to send over the network
Because kobo must always be kept as text

questions.q: Which is the best use of bigint in a shop's backend?
questions.explain: Bigints hold only integers, are slower, and do not mix with numbers. Use numbers for ordinary amounts checked with isSafeInteger, and bigints for aggregates and 64-bit values that need arithmetic.
options: Every price, because bigints are more precise
A yearly total of all transfers in kobo that can exceed 2<sup>53</sup>, where exact integer arithmetic on huge values is needed

questions.q: What happens when a calculation goes beyond Number.MAX_VALUE?
questions.explain: Floating-point overflow never throws. Validate results with Number.isFinite when inputs can be large.
options: The value wraps around to a negative number
The result becomes Infinity, silently, and further arithmetic carries it along
JavaScript switches to a bigint automatically

questions.q: Write nearlyEqual(a, b, relative = 1e-12) that returns true if a === b, or if the difference is at most relative times the larger absolute value.
questions.explain: The a === b check handles zeros (where the relative tolerance would be 0) and identical infinities. The relative part scales with the numbers.

questions.q: Write parseNairaToKobo(text) that accepts an optional ₦, commas as thousands separators and at most two decimals, and returns whole kobo, built from the digit strings (no multiplying a parsed decimal). Throw new Error("not an amount") otherwise.
questions.explain: padEnd(2, "0") turns ".5" into 50 kobo. Three decimals do not match the pattern, so "1.005" is rejected instead of silently rounded.
questions.expected:
125050
105
50
not an amount
not an amount

questions.q: Write divideHalfEven(numerator, denominator) for whole numbers and a positive denominator, rounding exact halves to the nearest even result and working for negative numerators too.
questions.explain: Compare twice the remainder with the denominator to classify the fraction exactly. For exact halves, keep an even quotient, otherwise move one step away from zero.

questions.q: Write formatKobo(kobo) that accepts a safe-integer number or a bigint, builds an exact decimal string with integer division and remainder, and formats it with an en-NG NGN currency formatter.
questions.explain: Converting to bigint gives one exact path for both input types. padStart(2, "0") turns 5 kobo into ".05".

questions.q: Write sumKobo(amounts) that throws a TypeError for any value that is not a safe integer, and a RangeError if the running total stops being a safe integer. The program prints the error names.
questions.explain: Number.isSafeInteger rejects fractions, strings, NaN and huge values in one check. Checking the running total catches overflow at the moment it happens.

questions.q: Serialise the refund object to JSON so that orderId (a bigint) becomes a JSON string with all its digits. Use a replacer function.
questions.explain: The replacer is called for every value; bigints become strings, everything else passes through. Readers in any language get the exact id.
questions.starter:
const refund = { orderId: 1844674407370955169n, amountKobo: 1250000 };

// print the JSON here
questions.solution:
const refund = { orderId: 1844674407370955169n, amountKobo: 1250000 };

console.log(JSON.stringify(refund, (key, value) => (typeof value === "bigint" ? value.toString() : value)));

questions.q: Write vatKobo(kobo, basisPoints) that computes VAT with integer maths and rounds exact halves away from zero (so 183.5 → 184). Print VAT at 7.5% (750 basis points) on 2,450 kobo, 2,460 kobo and 0 kobo.
questions.explain: 2,450 × 750 / 10,000 = 183.75 → 184; 2,460 × 750 / 10,000 = 184.5, an exact half → 185. Basis points keep everything in integers until the single rounding step.
